comparison: Strong agreement on dPAG neuronal responses to predator robot (C27-C29, C95-C99). Both evaluations find the electrophysiological and behavioral evidence compelling with appropriate controls. OpenEval emphasizes the lack of correlation with movement speed strengthens threat-specific interpretation; peer reviewers note 'solid evidence for the main claims.'

Strong agreement on optogenetic sufficiency evidence (C3, C22, C30-C34, C58, C100-C103). Both evaluations accept the frequency- and intensity-dependent behavioral effects and optrode validation. OpenEval highlights the dose-response relationships and control for fibers of passage; peer reviewers confirm findings without methodological concerns.

Partial overlap on dPAG stimulation activating BLA neurons (C4, C23). OpenEval groups these claims with behavioral similarity data (C35-C37, C104-C105) and notes the small percentage (10%) of responsive neurons. Peer R2 acknowledges the optogenetic activation of BLA but groups it differently with other optogenetic findings.

Strong agreement on dPAG-responsive BLA neurons showing enhanced predator responses (C38-C42, C65-C68, C106-C108, C111-C112). Both evaluations find the correlation analysis (r=0.405, p<0.001) and statistical comparisons between responsive and non-responsive cells compelling. Peer R3 emphasizes this supports dPAG conveying innate fear signals to amygdala.

Strong agreement on enhanced network coherence during predator encounters (C43-C45, C109-C110, C113-C120). Both evaluations accept the cross-correlation analyses showing heightened synchronous activity in dPAG-responsive BLA neurons. OpenEval provides detailed statistical validation; peer reviewers affirm the synchrony findings without concerns.

Strong agreement on PVT anatomical evidence (C7, C26, C46-C51, C73, C121-C125). Both evaluations find the c-Fos activation and triple-labeling data compelling while acknowledging this demonstrates correlation and connectivity, not necessity. Peer reviewers explicitly note the lack of functional behavioral assays as a limitation, consistent with OpenEval's assessment.

Complete agreement on limitation regarding necessity (C78). Both evaluations acknowledge that sufficiency has been demonstrated but necessity of the dPAG-PVT circuit has not been established. Peer R6 explicitly states 'the authors do not show if the PVT mediates dPAG to BLA communication with any functional behavioral assay.'

Agreement on methodological limitation regarding optogenetic plasticity (C72). Both evaluations accept this as appropriate scientific caution. OpenEval cites the relevant literature (Oishi et al., 2019); peer reviewers do not dispute this possibility and note it represents appropriate acknowledgment of potential confounds.

Strong agreement on background literature regarding fear conditioning (C1, C8-C16). Both evaluations accept these as established foundational claims that provide context for the current study. OpenEval notes appropriate citations to key studies; peer reviewers do not challenge these background concepts.

Agreement on distinction between innate and learned fear mechanisms (C62-C63, C84-C91). Both evaluations accept the conceptual framework and characterization of dPAG's role. OpenEval emphasizes the importance of this distinction for interpreting findings; peer reviewers accept these interpretive claims without challenge.

Agreement on prior clinical and experimental evidence (C17-C21). Both evaluations accept these citations as appropriate context. OpenEval notes the human intractable pain surgery data provides translational relevance; peer reviewers do not challenge these supporting claims from cited literature.

Agreement on specificity of dPAG responses to moving vs. stationary robots (C55-C57). Both evaluations accept this finding and its interpretation regarding looming stimuli. OpenEval notes the contrast with prior studies; peer reviewers do not challenge these interpretive claims.

Agreement on contextual differences in behavioral outcomes (C60-C61). Both evaluations accept the comparison with prior work (Deng et al., 2016) and the interpretation that environmental context influences behavioral expression. No concerns raised by either evaluation.

Agreement on broader neural circuitry context (C69, C75-C76, C79-C83). Both evaluations accept these citations establishing amygdala necessity and identifying other relevant brain regions. OpenEval notes these provide context for understanding broader circuitry; peer reviewers accept as supporting background claims.

Agreement on evolutionary and translational context (C52-C54). Both evaluations accept these claims providing broader context. OpenEval notes the human fMRI data provides translational relevance; peer reviewers accept without challenge as contextual claims.

Divergent assessment of therapeutic implications (C92-C94). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting C94's therapeutic suggestions are highly speculative and not supported by current data. Peer reviewers accept these as general discussion points without explicit critique, though Peer R3 notes the study 'brings important concepts' attractive to broad audience including psychiatrists.

Partial overlap on integrative model (C70, C74, C126-C127). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting the complete pathway has not been causally demonstrated despite plausible correlational evidence. Peer R5 accepts the anatomical evidence while noting limitations, consistent with OpenEval's caution about causal claims.

OpenEval identifies gap in literature (C2) regarding naturalistic predator encounters vs. Pavlovian conditioning paradigms. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addresses this gap identification, though it is implicit in their acceptance of the study's novelty.

OpenEval evaluates anatomical fact about lack of direct dPAG-BLA projections (C25). While peer R5 discusses PVT as potential mediator, no separate peer evaluation specifically addresses this foundational anatomical claim.

OpenEval evaluates citation about optogenetic-induced plasticity (C71, Oishi et al., 2019). While peer R9 accepts the limitation acknowledgment (C72), no separate peer evaluation addresses this specific citation as distinct from the limitation itself.
